items.text: According to Wealthtender research, the integration of technology into advisor search and service delivery has accelerated, with consumers now expecting digital-first experiences even for traditional services like financial advice.
items.quote: The integration of technology into advisor search and service delivery appears to have accelerated, with consumers now expecting digital-first experiences even for traditional services like financial advice.

items.text: One-third of survey participants said an advisor's physical location doesn't matter because they prefer to meet exclusively online, which Wealthtender describes as a fundamental change in how financial relationships can work.
items.quote: One-third of survey participants said an advisor's physical location doesn't matter because they prefer to meet exclusively online. This represents a fundamental change in how financial relationships can work.

items.text: Deloitte states that for clients the bar should rise quickly, with faster responses, more tailored insights, and more proactive outreach becoming minimum standards as agentic AI reshapes how advice is created, packaged, and delivered.
items.quote: For clients, the bar should rise quickly. Faster responses, more tailored insights, and more proactive outreach should become minimum standards.

items.text: Deloitte notes that clients want advice that is always on and frictionless, while advisers currently spend nearly 70% of their time on behind-the-scenes work rather than building client relationships.
items.quote: Clients want advice that's always on and frictionless, while advisers are busy managing larger, more complex books.

items.text: According to Capgemini, wealth management is shifting from product-centric distribution to empathy-led advice that extends beyond portfolios into the broader context of clients' lives.
items.quote: It explains how wealth management is shifting from product-centric distribution to empathy-led advice - advice that extends beyond portfolios into the broader context of clients' lives.

items.text: Adobe's Head of FS Jose Thomas states that technology will handle research and complexity, while advisors focus on judgment, empathy, and guiding clients through decisions that matter most.
items.quote: Technology will handle research and complexity, while advisors focus on judgment, empathy, and guiding clients through decisions that matter most.

items.text: Schwab CEO Richard Wurster notes that 77% of U.S. investors use AI today, though more than 90% still prefer human involvement in addition to AI.
items.quote: 77% of U.S. investors use AI today, though more than 90% still prefer human involvement in addition to AI.

items.text: Wealthtender states that the balance of technological enhancement with human oversight represents the future of financial advice.
items.quote: This balance of technological enhancement with human oversight represents the future of financial advice.

items.text: McKinsey states that AI will quickly replace tasks such as preparation, extraction, drafting, and scenario planning, especially in document-heavy planning and service work, but that replacing tasks is not the same as replacing the advisor's role as the human accountable for judgment, trust, and behavioral coaching.
items.quote: AI will quickly replace tasks such as preparation, extraction, drafting, and scenario planning, especially in document-heavy planning and service work. Replacing tasks is not the same as replacing the advisor's role as the human accountable for judgment, trust, and behavioral coaching.

items.text: According to CFPB research, Americans are more skeptical of information from generative AI and social media platforms than from qualified financial advisors, with 38% comfortable acting on financial information from a generative AI tool.
items.quote: They are more skeptical of information from generative AI and social media platforms... A generative AI tool (38%).
items.unit: Americans comfortable acting on financial information from a generative AI tool

items.text: Vanguard research found that 69% of digitally advised clients experienced significant increases in peace of mind, and that for digital advice the key attributes include transparency-visibility of portfolio changes, constant plan monitoring, round-the-clock online account access, trust, being on track to meet goals, and empowerment.
items.quote: For those using a digital advisor, 69% experienced significant increases in peace of mind... For digital advice, the key attributes are the need for transparency-visibility of portfolio changes, constant plan monitoring, round-the-clock and online account access, as well as trust and being on track to meet goals, along with empowerment.
items.unit: digitally advised clients reporting increased peace of mind

items.text: Schwab states that clients engage through in person, phone, web, mobile, or AI depending on their life stage and activity, and that every interaction combines 'the best of people and the power of AI.'
items.quote: At different times in their lives and for different activities, clients engage with us in person, on the phone, web, mobile, or via AI. Our clients value that flexibility. And in every interaction across every channel, we are bringing them an experience that combines the best of people and the power of AI

items.text: Schwab's CEO states AI opens up new distribution channels and allows creating personalized relationships with clients the firm could not serve with a person-to-person relationship.
items.quote: AI opens up new distribution channels and allows us to create personalized relationships with clients we have not been able to serve with a person-to- person relationship.

items.text: Schwab's CEO states retail clients seek holistic financial advice delivered 'seamlessly on their terms through a combination of people and increasingly AI-enabled technology.'
items.quote: more of our retail clients are seeking holistic financial advice delivered seamlessly on their terms through a combination of people and increasingly AI-enabled technology

items.text: Schwab's CEO states the firm harnesses AI 'the Schwab way,' bringing the best of people and technology and allowing clients to engage the way they prefer.
items.quote: we are harnessing the power of AI in the Schwab way, bringing the best of people and technology and allowing clients to engage the way they prefer

items.text: Schwab describes an AI capability that summarizes past client interactions, shares a view on helpful actions, records the client meeting, and prepares an action-based summary for the client.
items.quote: this capability quickly summarizes past client interactions using AI, shares a view on actions that would help the client, records the client meeting and prepares an action-based summary of the meeting for the client

items.text: Schwab's CEO states the future is 'Our people and AI working together to deliver better outcomes for clients.'

Raymond James, on the 4Q25 earnings call (period ended December 31, 2025), states it launched a proprietary digital AI operations agent named Rai that builds on its service-focused AI strategy.

Raymond James (trade press, published September 29, 2026) is piloting an AI-powered advisor assistant called Raimond, trained on approximately one million recorded calls between advisors and the firm's service center.

Schwab (investor day deck, published May 14, 2026) plans to leverage AI to allow reps to focus on deepening relationships through an enhanced advisor workstation, AI-enabled workflows, and pre-advice experiences to anticipate advice needs.

Schwab (investor day deck, published May 14, 2026) describes leveraging artificial intelligence to strengthen operational excellence and drive advisor success through delivering AI-powered advisor intelligence and enabling an open AI ecosystem.

Morgan Stanley's CEO, on the 3Q26 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2026), says technology can help do a lot of the early work for decisions clients make with their financial advisers on complex financial needs (parents, kids, philanthropy, taxes).

Raymond James (press release, published April 22, 2026, period ended March 31, 2026) states it continues to develop industry-leading technology solutions, including increasing AI integration, to improve efficiency and provide its financial professionals with more time to serve their clients.

Morgan Stanley, on the 2Q26 earnings call (period ended June 30, 2026), states it can offer financial advice broadly for different types of individuals at different points in their life cycle.

Schwab CEO Rick Wurster (trade press, published October 29, 2026) cites the need to make private-market investing more accessible to the masses as a focus area for its custody offerings.
Vanguard (Schwab trade press, published August 26, 2026) states its shared goal with Altruist is making investing and advice more affordable and accessible.
Schwab, on the 3Q26 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2026), states only about 5% of its retail households currently use an advice solution, while 31% say they are willing to pay for advice.

Morgan Stanley, on the 3Q26 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2026), states that of its bank-first clients, about one-third end up becoming a digital client or an adviser-based client over time, reflecting a broadening of access to advice from its banking relationships.

Schwab, on the 2Q26 earnings call (period ended June 30, 2026), states that just 5% of its retail households are in a fee-based advice solution while 31% of Schwab clients say they are willing to pay for advice, creating what it calls an unmatched conversion funnel into advice from its self-directed investor base.

Bank of America's Merrill Wealth Management and Private Bank (investor day deck, published November 5, 2025) identify multiple entry points into GWIM, including digital acquisition, enterprise introductions, workplace benefits, and advisor teams self-sourcing.

Bank of America (investor day deck, published November 5, 2025) describes its wealth management businesses as serving clients through all stages of the Wealth Continuum, from mass market (under $500K) through ultra high net worth ($10MM+), serving 4.7MM clients with 7% U.S. market share.

Edward Jones (10-K, period ended December 31, 2025) states its initiatives include targeting new clients through High Net Worth (expanded advice, planning, products and services), Workplace (connecting local business owners and their employees), and a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors.

Edward Jones (trade press, published September 30, 2026) says it wants to create opportunities for advisors to expand access to retirement plans for business owners who either don't have a plan today or have a smaller workforce.

Schwab, on the 4Q25 earnings call (period ended December 31, 2025), says its agreement to acquire Forge will help provide clients multiple ways to access alternatives while democratizing private investing.

McKinsey (published February 10, 2025) observes that firms across delivery models have been rolling out new advice propositions, with traditionally digital/direct wealth managers rapidly expanding their full-service advice offerings.
The CFPB (published June 6, 2025) notes that online platforms have expanded access to financial information, giving Americans more ways to build knowledge and improve their financial well-being.

Morgan Stanley, on the 3Q25 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2025), says its workplace channel is just scratching the surface, bringing in assets both as net new assets and directly into fee-based flows.

Morgan Stanley, on the 2Q26 earnings call (period ended June 30, 2026), states it is investing in referral models and products like LeadIQ to match individuals with advisers, aiming to become clients' principal financial adviser.

Edward Jones (10-K, period ended December 31, 2025) states that in Advisory Solutions, a client who elects to build a custom model has the investments selected by the client and their financial advisor, giving the client control over the account's investments.

Capgemini (published June 3, 2026) describes an Adaptive Experience AI Engine that dynamically tailors content depth, tone, and engagement pathways based on investor personas and life-event context, enabling personalized journeys in real time.

Merrill (press release, published September 15, 2026) states its Dollar Cost Averaging Service lets clients invest cash into eligible managed strategies over a predetermined, client-selected schedule, giving clients control over the timing of their investments.
Merrill (press release, published September 15, 2026) states its Tax Efficient Transition Service and Dollar Cost Averaging Service help support more personalized investment strategies for clients.

Vanguard (published June 4, 2025) identifies empowerment as a key attribute of digital advice, including a feeling of control over finances, awareness of fees, and a feeling that there is a path to financial freedom.

Schwab (investor day deck, published May 14, 2026) describes Schwab's Assistant as enabling clients to query personalized data and delivering in-session coaching, supporting client control and personalization.
Deloitte (published May 20, 2026) states that agentic AI should mean clients receive faster responses, more tailored insights, and more proactive outreach, raising the bar for the advice experience.

Edward Jones (10-K, period ended December 31, 2025) describes its Guided Solutions as a client-directed advisory program in which clients retain control over investment decisions, with advisors guiding them through identifying financial goals and selecting a portfolio objective.

Bank of America, on the 3Q26 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2026), says it believes strongly in keeping the human in the loop, because humans control their money and should control their money.

Bank of America, on the 3Q26 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2026), states it works with aggregators and agent providers to keep the customer in control of the decision, with the human remaining in the loop before money is moved out of their account.

Edward Jones (trade press, published August 18, 2026) notes that clients can be more proactively and productively engaged in the advice process when they have a better understanding of their own financial situation, enabled by personal financial management software.

Schwab, on the 2Q26 earnings call (period ended June 30, 2026), says capabilities are delivered in the ways clients want to interact—in person, phone, web, mobile, or via AI—and that clients value that flexibility.
Bank of America (investor day deck, published November 5, 2025) states its proprietary digital account onboarding solution allows advisor and client collaboration in real time digitally.

Schwab, on the 3Q26 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2026), states it is rolling out an AI managed capability to help clients think through their trading strategies, with the stated aim of empowering clients.
Schwab (investor day deck, published May 14, 2026) states its AI-generated portfolio insights translate portfolio data into tailored insights and possible actions for clients.

Capgemini (published June 3, 2026) states the future of wealth management will be defined by personalization at scale, with life transitions, liquidity events, and behavioral signals determining when and how firms interact with clients rather than calendar-driven reviews.
Bank of America (investor day deck, published November 5, 2025) lists deploying personalization capabilities based on client preferences among its key accelerants for wealth management.

A Capgemini research report (published June 3, 2026) describes a workspace that institutionalizes client intelligence by capturing client preferences, historical decisions and the rationale behind recommendations, and notes segment-based service prioritization so that digitally-savvy clients increasingly receive digital planning tools, automated insights and AI-driven service access.

Schwab (trade press, published October 23, 2026) states its integration of Syntax Direct with iRebal is meant to give RIAs control over creating personalized portfolios at scale, letting an advisor build a custom index and apply it across client accounts.

Edward Jones (10-K, period ended December 31, 2025) states its branch teams leverage new tools for deeper discovery conversations with clients and more comprehensive advice and planning.
Bank of America (10-K, period ended December 31, 2025) notes evolving client preferences have led to increased reliance on digital banking and other digital services.
McKinsey (published February 10, 2025), for the US advisor industry, projects that US advisor headcount will decline by about 0.2 percent annually.

McKinsey (published February 10, 2025), for the US advisor industry as of 2034, projects advisors needed by 2034 at 320 to 370 thousand, with a projected advisor count of 290 thousand based on current trends.

Deloitte (published May 20, 2026), for the wealth management industry as of 2032, predicts advisor productivity uplift (increase in advisor capacity from AI-driven time savings) could reach roughly 30% to 100% by 2032.
Bank of America's CEO, on the 4Q25 earnings call (period ended December 31, 2025), expects total company headcount to come down during 2026.

Morgan Stanley, on the 1Q25 earnings call (period ended March 31, 2025), reported a 3% reduction in XFA (financial advisor) headcount in Q1 2025 in Wealth Management and stated it has ongoing investments in automation and AI while assessing where people are needed over the next five to ten years.

Charles Schwab, on the 1Q25 earnings call (period ended March 31, 2025), expects to grow roughly 250 new financial and wealth consultants during 2025 and to continue investing in this through 2026 and 2027.

Charles Schwab, on the 1Q26 earnings call (period ended March 31, 2026), states it is continuing to hire financial consultants and wealth advisers while expanding its branch footprint, with about a dozen new branches planned for 2026.
McKinsey & Co. (trade press, published November 13, 2026), for the wealth management industry as of 2034, projects a shortfall of 90,000 to 110,000 advisors by 2034 at current productivity levels.
Schwab (trade press, published November 13, 2026) said the RIA industry would need to make 70,000 new hires by 2030 to keep up with current growth trends.

Mark Swan, CEO of Nevis (Schwab trade press, published October 30, 2026), said advisory firms partnering with Nevis are saving 10 hours a week per advisor on average, and that dozens of firms have frozen hiring.

caveats: All sources - How advisor headcount and staffing levels are projected to change with future advice delivery: the figures cover different bases and are not one series: US advisor industry: 2034; wealth management industry: 2032, 2034; Bank of America (total company headcount): 2026-09-30; Morgan Stanley Wealth Management: 2025-03-31; Charles Schwab: 2025; RIA industry: 2030. items.text: McKinsey believes fee pressure will be uneven, manifesting as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points, while anticipating a repricing of services where clients perceive no differentiation (such as basic tax projections).
items.quote: We believe fee pressure will be uneven, manifesting as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points.

items.text: McKinsey (PriceMetrix) reports that after a period of fee compression for advisory relationships from 2013 to 2018, fee rates have stabilized.
items.quote: After a period of fee compression for advisory relationships from 2013to 2018, fee rates havestabilized, according to PriceMetrix by McKinsey.

items.text: Cerulli states that for the past decade, financial firms have shifted their compensation models from largely commission-based to an asset-related fee structure.
items.quote: For the past decade, financial firms have shifted their compensation models from largely commission-based to an asset-related fee structure.

items.text: Cerulli finds that 33% of affluent investors compensate their provider via an asset-based fee, 21% use a no-fee platform, and 20% use a commission-based method, while 36% prefer a fee-based arrangement.
items.quote: Cerulli finds that 33% of affluent investors say they compensate their provider via an asset-based fee —just three percentage points lower than the 36% who indicated that they prefer this type of fee; 21% use a no-fee platform, and 20% use a commission-based method of payment

items.text: Deloitte states that lower cost-to-serve can expand margins for firms that maintain pricing, while competitive pressure may compress fees as planning outputs become easier to compare.
items.quote: Lower cost-to-serve can expand margins for firms that execute and maintain pricing. At the same time, competitive pressure may compress fees as planning outputs become easier to compare.

items.text: Kitces reports that 79% of surveyed advisor teams primarily derive client revenue from AUM fees.
items.quote: The majority of respondents (79%) work in teams that primarily derive client revenue from AUM fees.

items.text: Wealthtender's study finds 73% of survey participants consider transparency in fees and services the most important trust factor in an advisor.
items.quote: Nearly three-quarters (73%) of survey participants said transparency in fees and services is crucial for establishing an advisor's credibility.

items.text: Wealthtender's study finds lack of fee transparency was identified as a red flag by 38% of survey participants.
items.quote: Lack of fee transparency was identified as a red flag by 38% of survey participants.

items.text: Industry reporting states that platform tolls (data/support fees) at large distributors are directly or indirectly traceable to the zeroing out of commissions in the brokerage industry.
items.quote: all these platform tolls showing up at the giant distributors are directly or indirectly traceable to the zeroing out of commissions in the brokerage industry.

items.text: Industry reporting notes data analytics fees have become common among large distributors, with several peers having sold advisor data for years.
items.quote: Merrill is later than many of its peers [which] have sold advisor data for years

items.text: The debate over cash sweep transparency and pricing remains a live issue, with SEC focus on sweep disclosures and litigation over low client yields.
items.quote: the broader debate over cash sweep transparency and pricing remains a live issue. The SEC's sustained focus on sweep disclosures, combined with a wave of litigation against major firms over allegedly low client yields

items.text: Edward Jones notes ongoing fee compression across the mutual fund industry in recent years.
items.quote: driven in large part by the ongoing fee compression that has occurred across the mutual fund industry in recent years

items.text: Raymond James notes the market environment has resulted in a shift to passive investment products, which generate lower fees than actively managed products.
items.quote: the market environment in recent years has resulted in a shift to passive investment products, which generate lower fees than actively managed products.

items.text: Bank of America states it faces increasing pressure to provide products and services on more attractive terms, including lower fees, lower cost investment strategies and higher interest rates on deposits.
items.quote: Increasing pressure to provide products and services on more attractive terms, including lower fees, lower cost investment strategies and higher interest rates on deposits, may impact our ability to effectively compete.

items.text: Morgan Stanley states that in its Investment Management business, other investment managers and distributors continue to put downward pressure on fees.
items.quote: For certain products and geographies, we have experienced and will also likely continue to experience competitive pressures in our Investment Management business segment as other investment managers and distributors continue to put downward pressure on fees.

items.text: Edward Jones states the financial services industry is seeing an increasing number of firms providing lower cost, computer-based robo-advice.
items.quote: with an increasing number of firms of all sizes providing personalized services and enhanced digital experiences for clients, including the utilization of artificial intelligence technologies and lower cost, computer-based "robo-advice".

items.text: Edward Jones states it is subject to competition from robo-advisors and other lower cost options and from fintech companies with internet- and mobile-based platforms.
items.quote: The Partnership is also subject to competition in the industry from robo-advisors and other lower cost options and from "fintech" companies with internet- and mobile-based platforms

items.text: Morgan Stanley states it continues to experience price competition in some businesses as electronic execution and new technologies put pressure on revenues.
items.quote: We continue to experience price competition in some of our businesses. In particular, the ability to execute securities, derivatives and other financial instrument trades electronically ... will likely continue the pressure on revenues.

items.text: Cerulli Associates data shows the number of fee-only RIAs at the $5 billion level grew 7.8% over five years.
items.quote: the number of fee-only RIAs at the $5 billion level jumped 7.8% over five years

items.text: Schwab states its model is informed by investors' preferences for lower explicit fees without sacrificing product access, convenience or service.
items.quote: Our model is informed by investors' preferences for lower explicit fees without sacrificing product access, convenience or service.

items.text: Schwab's CEO states the firm adapted as commissions went down.
items.quote: just as we figured it out as commissions went down, we'll figure it out if the economics change in this environment.

items.text: A consumer survey found nearly half of participants (48%) said pricing and overall anticipated costs are among the top three factors leading them to choose one advisor over another.
items.quote: Nearly half of survey participants (48%) said pricing and overall anticipated costs are among the top three factors that lead them to choose one advisor over others.

items.text: Research recommends advisors develop clear, comprehensive fee explanation pages to ensure prospects understand what services may cost before engaging.
items.quote: Fee Structure Pages: Develop clear, comprehensive fee explanations to ensure prospects feel confident they understand what your services may cost before the engage with you further.

items.text: Merrill Lynch is creating new 'data' and 'shelf' fees (fee bundles) that third-party managers pay for listing and visibility with its advisors.
items.quote: Merrill Lynch is creating a way ... for third-party managers to get listed, seen by, and even "recommended" by "thundering herd" brokers ... it's a menu of choices presented to brokers who are shopping investments for their clients. But the privilege won't come cheap.

Some items concern data-fee introduction timing (trade press reports Charles Schwab introduced data fees over seven years ago, UBS in the mid-2010s, and Merrill Lynch later than many peers), others concern data-fee rate levels (Morgan Stanley between $25,000 and $500,000 versus Merrill's $125,000 to $860,000), and still others concern regulatory settlements of differing amounts and dates (Charles Schwab $187 million in 2022, Raymond James $13 million in July 2023, Wells Fargo and Merrill $4.4 million, Edward Jones $320,754.72 per state), so no valid ranking of firms as leading or lagging can be constructed from this evidence.

duplicates_removed.text: Industry reporting (trade press, published September 30, 2026) states that in 2026 the debate over cash sweep transparency and pricing remains a live issue, with SEC focus on sweep disclosures and litigation over low client yields.

A consumer survey (research published August 13, 2025) found that 48% of participants said pricing and overall anticipated costs are among the top three factors leading them to choose one advisor over another.

McKinsey (research published April 8, 2026) states its belief that fee pressure will be uneven, manifesting as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points.
Wealthtender's study (published August 13, 2025) notes that many advisors avoid discussing fees upfront, creating an opportunity for transparent advisors.

Deloitte (research published May 20, 2026) notes that competitive pressure may compress fees as planning outputs become easier to compare. Why it might matter: in the same passage Deloitte states that lower cost-to-serve can expand margins for firms that execute and maintain pricing, so the outcome is margin expansion for some and pressure for others.

Schwab (1Q26 earnings call) states that its model is informed by investors' preferences for lower explicit fees without sacrificing product access, convenience or service. Why it might matter: in the same earnings-call passage Schwab states it has a lot of flexibility to continue supporting investors and RIAs if those preferences change in the future.

McKinsey (research published April 8, 2026) states it believes fee pressure will be uneven, manifesting as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points. Why it might matter: in the same passage McKinsey notes that fee rates for relationships of more than $1 million have remained remarkably steady at about 104 basis points since 2019 even as digital tools proliferated.

McKinsey (research published April 8, 2026) expects fee pressure to be uneven, manifesting as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points. Why it might matter: in the same passage McKinsey notes that fee rates for relationships of more than $1 million have remained remarkably steady at about 104 basis points since 2019 even as digital tools proliferated.

Edward Jones's 2025 Form 10-K states it is subject to competition from robo-advisors and other lower-cost options and from fintech companies. Why it might matter: in the same passage Edward Jones states that if it cannot keep pace with this rapidly changing environment and meet client needs, it could lose clients, thereby reducing revenues.

Bank of America's 2025 Form 10-K states it faces increasing pressure to provide products and services on more attractive terms, including lower fees and lower-cost investment strategies. Why it might matter: in the same passage Bank of America states it operates in a highly competitive environment with intense competition from bank and nonbank financial institutions and new market entrants, and that this pricing pressure may impact its ability to effectively compete.

Raymond James's 2025 Form 10-K states that in fixed income and equity markets, regulatory requirements have resulted in greater price transparency, leading to price competition and decreased trading margins. Why it might matter: in the same passage Raymond James states that its trading margins have been further compressed by the shift from high- to low-touch services over time, and it believes price competition and pricing pressures in these and other areas will continue.

A study (published August 13, 2025) shows 73% of people consider fee transparency the most important trust factor. Why it might matter: the same passage advises always asking for a clear, written explanation of all costs before engaging an advisor, and notes that lack of fee transparency was identified as a red flag by 38% of survey participants.

a1.EDJ.label: not_found
a1.EDJ.reason: None of the passages discuss younger investors or clients under 40 or their product, service, or channel preferences; all passages concern accounting matters such as fee revenue recognition, fair value measurements, contingencies, advisory program descriptions, and operating expenses.

first.label: not_found
first.reason: The passages describe the firm's initiatives (a new digital platform targeting Next Generation investors, investments in technology) and general statements about changing client expectations, but none states what product, service, or channel preferences younger investors or clients under 40 actually express.

a2.EDJ.label: not_found
a2.EDJ.reason: None of the passages discuss what communication or engagement channels younger investors prefer; they concern technology infrastructure, banking, financial statements, and partnership structure.

first.label: not_found
first.reason: None of the passages state what communication and engagement channels younger investors prefer; the only related mentions are Edward Jones's own initiatives (a digital platform for Next Generation investors) and general statements about changing demographics and digital experiences, not a statement of younger investors' preferred channels.

a3.EDJ.label: fact

items.text: Edward Jones states that one of its new-client initiatives is "a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors," indicating the firm is targeting younger investors through a digital service model rather than its traditional full-service branch model.
items.quote: a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors

items.text: Edward Jones states its continued ability to compete may be adversely impacted by "generational wealth transfer, including changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs, and changing client demographics, preferences and values," pointing to evolving preferences among younger/demographically shifting clients toward technology and expanded offerings.
items.quote: generational wealth transfer, including changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs, and changing client demographics, preferences and values

a3.EDJ.reason: The passages give partial, firm-framed evidence about younger (Next Generation) investors' orientation toward digital platforms and technology, but do not explicitly state a self-directed versus full-service preference.

a4.EDJ.label: not_found
a4.EDJ.reason: None of the passages mention growth in younger investors or clients under 40; they cover partnership/exhibit lists, partner counts, revenue/expense notes, trade revenue, net new assets, and financial advisor headcounts.

first.label: not_found
first.reason: No passage reports any growth figure for younger investors or clients under 40; passages reference an 'aging client base' and a digital platform targeting 'Next Generation investors' as an initiative, but state no growth metric.

a5.EDJ.label: fact

items.text: Edward Jones states it is pursuing a new digital platform initiative, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors, as one of several initiatives to meet clients' planning, investing, saving, spending, borrowing and comprehensive needs.
items.quote: These initiatives also include targeting new clients: High Net Worth, focused on attracting and serving high net worth clients through expanded advice, planning, products and services across multiple service models; Workplace, which connects local business owners and their employees with financial solutions through their workplace; and a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors.

items.text: Edward Jones announced it has taken a minority stake in the personal finance app Quicken, with the stated intention of integrating Quicken's personal financial management capabilities more directly into Edward Jones to support its value proposition and advisor conversations with clients, though the firm notes it is still determining its actual deployment strategy.
items.quote: Edward Jones announced that they have taken a minority stake in the personal finance app Quicken, with an explicit intention that the investment is a step towards integrating Quicken's personal financial management capabilities more directly into Edward Jones as a way to support their value proposition and advisor conversations with clients.

a5.EDJ.reason: The passages state current/recent digital initiatives, including a digital platform explicitly aimed at Next Generation investors and a technology investment to enhance digital personal financial management, which bear on alignment with younger investors' preferences.

a6.EDJ.label: fact

items.text: Edward Jones states that its initiatives to meet clients' planning, investing, saving, spending, borrowing and comprehensive needs include targeting new clients, including a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors.
items.quote: These initiatives also include targeting new clients: High Net Worth, focused on attracting and serving high net worth clients through expanded advice, planning, products and services across multiple service models; Workplace, which connects local business owners and their employees with financial solutions through their workplace; and a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors.

items.text: Edward Jones states its strategic ambition includes anticipating clients' needs with the right offering at the right time, now and for generations to come, and attracting and serving new client segments.
items.quote:
Anticipate clients' needs with the right offering at the right time, now and for generations to come

• Attract and serve new client segments

items.text: Edward Jones states its continued ability to compete and adapt its business model may be adversely impacted by generational wealth transfer and changing client demographics, preferences and values, including changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs.
items.quote: The Partnership's continued ability to compete and adapt its business model may be adversely impacted by the evolving financial services industry and generational wealth transfer, including changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs, and changing client demographics, preferences and values.

items.text: Edward Jones states it addresses strategic risks, most notably competition for clients and personnel in light of the evolving financial services industry and generational wealth transfer, and changing client demographics, preferences and values, through initiatives to deliver enhanced value and impact.
items.quote: The Partnership seeks to address its strategic risks, most notably competition for clients and personnel in light of the evolving financial services industry and generational wealth transfer, changing client demographics, preferences and values, technology, artificial intelligence, and regulatory changes, through its initiatives to deliver enhanced value and impact for millions of current and potential clients, colleagues and communities.

a6.EDJ.reason: The passages state Edward Jones's strategy and priorities relevant to younger/next-generation and new client segments, including a digital platform for Next Generation investors and attention to generational wealth transfer and changing demographics.

a8.EDJ.label: fact

items.text: Edward Jones's initiatives to target new clients include a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors.
items.quote: a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors

items.text: The Partnership seeks to address its strategic risks, including generational wealth transfer and changing client demographics, preferences and values, through its initiatives.
items.quote: most notably competition for clients and personnel in light of the evolving financial services industry and generational wealth transfer, changing client demographics, preferences and values

items.text: The Partnership's ability to compete may be adversely impacted by generational wealth transfer and changing client demographics, preferences and values, including changing expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs.
items.quote: the evolving financial services industry and generational wealth transfer, including changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs, and changing client demographics, preferences and values

a8.EDJ.reason: The passages state Edward Jones's own disclosures and initiative (a digital platform for Next Generation investors) and its disclosures about generational wealth transfer and changing demographics, which bear on younger investors.

a1.SCHW.label: fact

items.text: Younger investors learn about finances primarily through social media and family, and Schwab meets them in the channels where they turn for information about investing.
items.quote: One of the reasons they're turning to Schwab is because we're meeting them in the channels where they turn for information about investing. We know they learn about finances primarily through social media and family.

items.text: The top online resource for younger investors learning about finances is YouTube.
items.quote: Their top online resource is YouTube, and we're the number one financial services firm on YouTube by followers.

items.text: One-third of retail households that created a financial plan within the last two years are under the age of 40, indicating younger investors' engagement with financial planning services.
items.quote: one-third of retail households who created a financial plan within the last two years are under the age of 40
items.unit: retail households who created a financial plan within the last two years

items.text: Younger investors want to think about how to pay off their college debt and how to buy a house.
items.quote: young investors who want to think about how to pay off their college debt, how to buy a house

items.text: Younger traders turn to Schwab because they recognize the potential of trading to help build wealth over time and for the platforms, tools, education, coaching, expertise, and service Schwab provides.
items.quote: Younger traders are turning to us because they recognize the potential that trading has in helping build wealth over time. And they are turning to Schwab because we have the platforms, tools, education, coaching, expertise, and service they need to help them succeed

items.text: 42% of thinkorswim users are Millennial or Gen Z, indicating engagement with the thinkorswim trading platform among younger investors.
items.quote: 42% of thinkorswim→ users are Millennial or Gen Z

items.text: According to the CEO, crypto will appeal to young investors.
items.quote: Crypto will be great for clients and will certainly appeal to young investors.

a1.SCHW.reason: The passages state several product, service, and channel preferences of younger investors and clients under 40: they learn about finances through social media, family, and YouTube (channels); they create financial plans and want help with college debt and home buying (services); and they turn to Schwab for trading platforms/tools, thinkorswim, and crypto (products).

a2.SCHW.label: fact

items.text: Schwab states that younger investors (Gen Z) learn about finances primarily through social media and family.
items.quote: We know they learn about finances primarily through social media and family.

items.text: Schwab states that younger investors' top online resource is YouTube, and that Schwab is the number one financial services firm on YouTube by followers.
items.quote: Their top online resource is YouTube, and we're the number one financial services firm on YouTube by followers.

items.text: Schwab states it is meeting younger investors in the channels where they turn for information about investing.
items.quote: One of the reasons they're turning to Schwab is because we're meeting them in the channels where they turn for information about investing.

a2.SCHW.reason: The passages explicitly state the communication/engagement channels younger investors prefer (social media, family, YouTube), so these are facts.

a3.SCHW.label: fact

items.text: Schwab's investor-day framework groups 'Younger investors' with self-directed offerings—Schwab Starter Kit, Schwab Teen Investor Account, and no/low commissions—and lists full-service advice (Wealth Advisory, Advisor Network, Managed accounts) under a separate 'Advice seekers' segment.
items.quote: Younger investors | Schwab Starter Kit TM | Schwab Teen Investor TM Account | No / low commissions

items.text: Schwab states younger traders turn to Schwab because it offers the platforms, tools, education, coaching, expertise, and service they need to help them succeed (a self-directed-with-support model).
items.quote: Younger traders are turning to us because they recognize the potential that trading has in helping build wealth over time. And they are turning to Schwab because we have the platforms, tools, education, coaching, expertise, and service they need to help them succeed

items.text: Schwab reports that one-third of retail households who created a financial plan within the last two years are under age 40, indicating younger investors are a minority among those using financial planning (an advice service).
items.quote: one-third of retail households who created a financial plan within the last two years are under the age of 40
items.unit: retail households who created a financial plan in the last two years

a3.SCHW.reason: No passage states an explicit 'self-directed versus full-service' preference, but passages associate younger investors with self-directed offerings (no/low commissions, Starter Kit, Teen Investor, trading platforms/tools/education) and show them as a minority among financial-plan users, so I label this as a partial fact.

a4.SCHW.label: fact

items.text: Schwab reports that approximately 70% of new-to-firm retail households are Gen Z and millennials.

claims.text: The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 3Q25 earnings call (October 2025), management said younger investors learn about finances primarily through social media and family, and that Schwab is meeting them in the channels where they turn for information about investing.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 3Q25 earnings call (October 2025), management said younger investors' top online resource for learning about finances is YouTube, and that Schwab is 'the number one financial services firm on YouTube by followers.'
The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 2Q25 earnings call (July 2025), management said young investors want to think about how to pay off their college debt and how to buy a house.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 3Q25 earnings call (October 2025), management said younger traders turn to Schwab because they recognize the potential of trading to help build wealth over time, and for the platforms, tools, education, coaching, expertise, and service Schwab provides.
The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 3Q25 earnings call (October 2025), the CEO said crypto 'will certainly appeal to young investors.'

Industry research: A Bank of America Private Bank study (published June 2026) reports that younger investors (Gen Z and Millennials, ages 21 to 45) are reshaping how wealth is built and diversified, embracing alternative investments and emerging technologies.
Industry research: The same study reports that 67% of younger investors (ages 21 to 45) believe traditional stocks and bonds can no longer deliver above-average returns.

Industry research: The study reports that younger investors allocate nearly half as much to stocks as older generations, while allocating more to alternatives (15%) and crypto (13%) than older investors.

Industry research: The study reports that crypto ranks as the #1 wealth-creation opportunity for young wealthy investors: 29% rank it #1, 58% currently own crypto (up from 49% in 2024), and 92% either own or are interested.
Industry research: The study reports that 88% of younger investors say they are likely to allocate more to alternatives in the next few years, compared with just 15% of Boomers and Silents.

Industry research: FINRA investor research (published December 2025) reports that younger investors (under 35) are much more likely to own individual stocks than mutual funds (82 percent vs. 47 percent).

Industry research: FINRA investor research (published December 2025) reports that younger investors (ages 18-34) are much more likely than older investors to have an options trading account (68%) and to have traded options (43%).

Industry research: FINRA investor research (published December 2025) reports that younger respondents are much more likely than older respondents to invest for reasons other than long-term profits; half or more of those under 35 say they invest for social responsibility, entertainment, and social activity reasons.

Industry research: FINRA investor research (published December 2025) reports that among those who have purchased meme stocks or other viral investments, 66% cite entertainment and 65% social activity as reasons for investing.

Industry research: A Bank of America Private Bank study (published June 2024) reports that younger investors (ages 21 to 43) believe it is no longer possible to achieve above-average investment returns by investing solely in traditional stocks and bonds, a view held by a much smaller share of investors over age 44.

Industry research: The same study reports that among younger high-net-worth investors (ages 21 to 43), 47% of portfolios are in stocks and bonds (vs 74% for over-44), 17% is allocated to alternatives, 93% plan to allocate more to alternatives, and 49% own cryptocurrencies.

Comparison: Edward Jones's younger-investor disclosures are forward-looking and initiative-based—a new digital platform targeting Next Generation investors, an acknowledgment of generational wealth transfer as a strategic risk, and a minority stake in Quicken—whereas Schwab discloses detailed quantitative metrics on younger-client acquisition (for example, approximately 70% of new-to-firm retail households being Gen Z and millennials as of 3Q26) and names specific younger-investor offerings (Schwab Starter Kit, Schwab Teen Investor Account, no/low commissions, YouTube, crypto). Merrill's and Raymond James's cited materials concern next-generation financial advisors (recognition lists and a next-gen advisor recruiting strategy) rather than younger investors or clients, and Morgan Stanley's disclosures were not found; the quantitative metrics are therefore not comparable across firms (different definitions and scopes), so the comparison can be made only qualitatively at the level of disclosures and initiatives.

a1.all.label: fact

items.text: UBS research reports that experience and expertise sit at the top of the next generation's wish list when choosing a wealth manager, cited by 79% of respondents.
items.quote: When choosing a wealth manager, experience and expertise sit at the top of the next generation's wish list (79%).

items.text: Cerulli reports that financial advisors seeking to connect with Millennial prospective clients must be able to articulate benefits outside of the investing realm, such as financial planning, lending, and tax services.
items.quote: financial advisors looking to connect with these prospective clients must be able to articulate benefits outside of the investing realm, such as financial planning, lending, and tax services.

items.text: Cerulli notes younger investors prefer to retain a greater degree of control over at least part of their investing lives.
items.quote: younger investors prefer to retain a greater degree of control of at least part of their investing lives.

items.text: Bank of America Private Bank's 2026 study reports 65% of young investors still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor.
items.quote:
sixty five percent
65%
still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor.

items.text: A WealthTender survey found that 73% of people consider fee transparency the most important trust factor when engaging an advisor.
items.quote: Our study shows 73% of people consider fee transparency the most important trust factor.

items.text: A WealthTender survey found the most helpful information when looking for a financial advisor is pricing and fees (70.6%) and years of experience and education (70.8%), followed by specialization (61.0%), professional certifications/credentials (59.6%), and responsiveness/communication style (59.4%).
items.quote: Pricing and fees 70.60%... Years of experience and education 70.80%... Specialization (e.g., retirement planning, business owners) 61.00%... Professional certifications/credentials (e.g., CFP, CFA) 59.60%... Responsiveness and communication style 59.40%

items.text: People actively considering hiring a financial advisor rely on reviews from actual clients, prefer to speak directly with the advisor (72% visit the advisor's website, 73% schedule an introductory call), and more than half (55%) plan to seek second opinions from others who know the advisors on their shortlist.
items.quote: Reviews from actual clients can give you insights... Nearly three-quarters of people want to speak with an advisor directly... 72% of people will visit the advisor's website... 73% will schedule an introductory call... More than half (55%) of survey participants also plan to seek second opinions
items.scope: U.S. adults with household incomes over $100,000, ages 35-64, who don't have or are considering changing advisors

items.text: The survey of factors in searching for and hiring an advisor covered 500 U.S. adults with household incomes over $100,000, ages 35-64, screened to include only those who don't currently have an advisor or are considering a change and anticipate hiring within five years.
items.quote: The study surveyed 500 U.S. adults with household incomes over $100,000, selected from a larger pool of 1,557 individuals who met basic demographic criteria (ages 35-64, $100K+ household income). Participants were screened to include only those who either don't currently have a financial advisor or have one but are considering a change, and who anticipate hiring an advisor within the next five years.

items.text: Among younger investors (Gen Z and Millennials, ages 21 to 45), 65% prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor, while 87% are comfortable with advisors using AI to help manage portfolios.
items.quote: sixty five percent 65% still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor... eighty seven percent 87% are comfortable with advisors using AI to help manage portfolios
items.scope: younger investors (Gen Z and Millennials, ages 21 to 45)

a1.all.reason: Multiple passages provide direct survey evidence on the factors younger and next-generation clients consider when choosing a financial advisor.

a2.all.label: fact

items.text: The CFPB reports that younger Americans are far more likely than older Americans to embrace social media, podcasts and generative AI to meet their financial information needs.
items.quote: Younger Americans are far more likely to embrace social media, podcasts and generative AI to meet their financial information needs.

items.text: The CFPB reports that Americans aged 25-45 are more trusting than older Americans aged 46-64 of financial information obtained from generative AI tools (44% vs. 26%).
items.quote: Those aged 25-45 are more trusting than older Americans aged 4664 of the financial information obtained from generative AI tools (44% vs. 26%) and social media (44% vs. 24%).

items.text: FINRA reports that among young investors, word of mouth from friends/family/colleagues is the most frequently mentioned source of investment information, used by 85 percent of investors under 35.
items.quote: Among young investors, word of mouth from friends/family/colleagues is the most frequently mentioned source of investment information, used by 85 percent of investors under 35.

items.text: Schwab's CEO states that Gen Z investors learn about finances primarily through social media and family.
items.quote: We know they learn about finances primarily through social media and family.

items.text: A Goldman Sachs Asset Management survey reports that Millennials cite social media more often as a source of information on alternatives, while Boomers rely on traditional outlets.
items.quote: Millennials cite social media more often, while Boomers rely on traditional outlets.

items.text: Schwab CEO Rick Wurster states that younger investors' top online resource is YouTube, where Schwab is the number one financial services firm by followers, and that younger investors at Schwab are highly engaged in building wealth over the long term.
items.quote: Their top online resource is YouTube, and we're the number one financial services firm on YouTube by followers. And younger investors at Schwab are highly engaged in building their wealth over the long term.

items.text: Wealthtender's 2025 study of high-income households found that 83% of consumers will research an advisor's reputation online and specifically want to read online reviews.
items.quote: 83% of consumers will research you reputation online, and specifically indicated they want to read online reviews.
items.unit: of consumers who research advisor's reputation online and want to read online reviews
items.scope: U.S. adults ages 35-64 with $100K+ household income, actively seeking or considering an advisor

items.text: Wealthtender's 2025 study found that 72% of people will visit the advisor's website to continue their research.
items.quote: 72% of people will visit the advisor's website to continue their research, while a nearly identical number of people (73%) will schedule an introductory call.
items.unit: of people who will visit the advisor's website
items.scope: U.S. adults ages 35-64 with $100K+ household income, actively seeking or considering an advisor

a2.all.reason: These passages state, with age breakdowns, the channels and sources (social media, generative AI, podcasts, word of mouth/friends-family, financial professionals) that younger clients use for financial/investment information and advisor-related decisions.

a3.all.label: fact

items.text: In the 2025 Wealthtender Voice of the Client Study, the top 2-3 most important financial goals or needs respondents said they would seek a financial advisor's help with were retirement planning and income strategies (63%), investment management and portfolio growth (53%), tax planning and optimization (29%), and estate planning and wealth transfer (26%).
items.quote: What are your top 2-3 most important financial goals or needs that you would seek a financial advisor's help with?... Retirement planning and income strategies 63... Investment management and portfolio growth 53... Tax planning and optimization 29... Estate planning and wealth transfer 26

items.text: The Wealthtender study found that nearly 90% of client reviews about financial advisors focus on relationship quality, planning advice, and emotional factors, while only 1 in 10 centers on investments or portfolio management.
items.quote: nearly 90% of client reviews written about financial advisors focus on relationship quality, planning advice, and emotional factors, while only 1 in 10 reviews centers on investments or portfolio management

items.text: In a Goldman Sachs Asset Management survey, the top three most important investment goals for Millennials (born early 1980s-mid-1990s) were to grow wealth over time, plan for comfortable or early retirement, and achieve financial independence.
items.quote: Millennials (born early 1980s-mid-1990s)... Grow wealth over time | Plan for comfortable or early retirement | Financial independence

items.text: Goldman Sachs Asset Management's retirement survey found that major life events such as having a child, buying a home, funding college, or managing a significant financial hardship are especially common among younger cohorts: 66% of Gen Z and 59% of Millennials reported experiencing at least one major life event in the prior 24 months.
items.quote: Of working respondents, 66% of Gen Z and 59% of Millennials experienced at least one major life event in the past 24 months.
items.scope: Gen Z and Millennial working respondents

items.text: Goldman Sachs Asset Management reported a generational divide in how competing financial priorities (credit card debt, paying down student loans, saving for college, caring for family members, time out of the workforce, financial hardship) affect retirement savings, with Generation X, Millennials, and Generation Z reporting significantly higher impact than Baby Boomers, and Millennials the most impacted.
items.quote: Younger generations, specifically Generation X, Millennials, and Generation Z, consistently report a significantly higher impact from these challenges compared to Baby Boomers. Millennials, for instance, are noted as being the most impacted.
items.scope: Generation X, Millennials, Generation Z vs. Baby Boomers

items.text: Cerulli found that younger investors typically are more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages, meaning financial advisors looking to connect with these prospective clients must be able to articulate benefits outside of the investing realm, such as financial planning, lending, and tax services.
items.quote: Younger investors typically are more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages (e.g., E*TRADE, Fidelity), meaning financial advisors looking to connect with these prospective clients must be able to articulate benefits outside of the investing realm, such as financial planning, lending, and tax services.

items.text: Fidelity's 2025 Investor Insights Study found that generation X, Y, and Z investors are reshaping the advisor-client relationship with a focus on holistic financial planning, life goal achievement, and non-traditional investment strategies, and that these wealthy next-generation households seek transparency in advisor compensation and broader life guidance beyond investment management.
items.quote: generation X, Y, and Z investors are reshaping the advisor-client relationship with a focus on holistic financial planning, life goal achievement, and non-traditional investment strategies... these high-net-worth households seek transparency in advisor compensation, broader life guidance beyond investment management
items.scope: wealthy next generation (Gen X, Y, Z) households

items.text: A UBS next generation study found that when choosing a wealth manager, experience and expertise sit at the top of the next generation's wish list (79%), while more than half (56%) want advisors who can build trusted relationships across generations, and 41% value the ability to fully understand the next generation's needs.
items.quote: experience and expertise sit at the top of the next generation's wish list (79%)... More than half (56%) want advisors who can build trusted relationships across generations... ability to fully understand the next generation's needs (41%)

items.text: A UBS next generation study found that two-thirds (67%) of next generation investors say a strong personal connection with their advisor is important, and that women place greater weight on personal fit and regular contact while men focus on competitive pricing and specialist expertise.
items.quote: Two-thirds (67%) say a strong personal connection with their advisor is important... Women place greater weight on personal fit and regular contact, while men focus on competitive pricing and specialist expertise.

items.text: A Bank of America Private Bank 2026 Study of Wealthy Americans found that among younger married investors planning is starting earlier: 32% of Gen Z and Millennials have a prenuptial agreement (with another 15% planning to), compared with 15% of Gen X and 4% of Boomers and Silents.
items.quote: Among younger married investors, planning is starting earlier: thirty two percent 32% of Gen Z and Millennials have a prenuptial agreement (with another fifteen percent 15% planning to), compared with fifteen percent 15% of Gen X and four percent 4% of Boomers and Silents.
items.scope: Gen Z and Millennials vs Gen X and Boomers/Silents

items.text: Schwab's CEO Rick Wurster stated that young new-to-firm households (one in three of which are under age 24) come to Schwab wanting to consolidate loans into a Pledged Asset Line to pay off student debt, discuss how to buy a house in the future, and be investors for the long term.
items.quote: One in three of our new-to-firm household numbers, which are really strong new-to-firm numbers, are under the age of 24... They'll come in and want to consolidate loans into a Pledged Asset Line balance so they can pay off their student debt. They'll talk to us about how to buy a house in the future. These are clients that really want to be investors for the long term

items.text: Schwab's CEO Rick Wurster said young investors come to Schwab wanting to think about how to pay off their college debt and how to buy a house.
items.quote: young investors who want to think about how to pay off their college debt, how to buy a house, there's no better place to be than here at Schwab

items.text: Bank of America's investor day cites McKinsey 2024 survey data that 70% of investors with $250K+ in assets aged 25-44 are looking to transfer investment assets to a bank within the next 12 months, indicating a priority among young investors to consolidate their investments and banking relationships.
items.quote: 70% of $250K+ investors aged 25-44 are looking to transfer investment assets to a bank within the next 12 months.
items.unit: percent of investors aged 25-44 with $250K+ in assets
items.scope: investors aged 25-44 with $250K+ in assets (McKinsey survey)

a3.all.reason: Multiple research and industry passages state financial priorities and life-stage needs (retirement planning, wealth growth, major life events, holistic planning, relationship quality) that shape how younger/next-generation clients evaluate and choose advisors.

a4.all.label: fact

items.text: In the UBS Next Generation study, when the next generation chooses a wealth manager, 'Digital savviness' was named by 21% of respondents as a quality a wealth manager should possess, ranking well below experience and expertise (79%) and commitment to next generation (56%); the study notes that 'technical capability alone isn't enough'.
items.quote: What qualities should a wealth manager/private banker possess in order to properly advise you? (in %) ... Digital savviness ... 21 ... Technical capability alone isn't enough. More than half (56%) want advisors who can build trusted relationships across generations.

items.text: Among younger adults, those aged 25-45 are more trusting than older Americans aged 46-64 of financial information obtained from generative AI tools (44% vs 26%) and social media (44% vs 24%).
items.quote: Those aged 25-45 are more trusting than older Americans aged 4664 of the financial information obtained from generative AI tools (44% vs. 26%) and social media (44% vs. 24%).
items.unit: % of those aged 25-45 trusting financial info (generative AI and social media)

items.text: Among consumers seeking a financial advisor, 96% said they will do further research online before making a hiring decision, and 83% will research an advisor's reputation by looking for online reviews and awards.
items.quote: 96% will do further research online before making a hiring decision ... the most popular next step for 83% of respondents is to research the advisor's reputation by looking for online reviews and awards
items.unit: % of respondents doing online research before hiring
items.scope: consumers seeking a financial advisor (Wealthtender study)

items.text: One-third of survey participants said an advisor's physical location doesn't matter because they prefer to meet exclusively online.
items.quote: One-third of survey participants said an advisor's physical location doesn't matter because they prefer to meet exclusively online.
items.scope: consumers seeking a financial advisor (Wealthtender study)

items.text: The study describes consumers researching potential advisors using search engines like Google, advisor directories like Wealthtender, and AI tools like ChatGPT.
items.quote: rch potential advisors, including search engines like Google, advisor directories like Wealthtender, and AI tools like ChatGPT
items.scope: consumers seeking a financial advisor (Wealthtender study)

items.text: The study anticipates continued growth in AI tool usage for advisor searches, increasing expectation for faster response times and digital-first communications, and further acceptance of virtual advisor relationships.
items.quote: Continued growth in AI tool usage for advisor searches ... Increasing expectation for faster response times and digital-first communications ... Further acceptance of virtual advisor relationships regardless of geographic location
items.scope: consumers seeking a financial advisor (Wealthtender study)

items.text: Wealthtender's 2025 study found that 25% of people plan to use AI-powered tools like ChatGPT or Gemini to start their search for a financial advisor.
items.quote: 25% of people plan to use ChatGPT, Gemini or other AI-powered tools to start their advisor search

a4.all.reason: The passages directly state how under-40 (next generation / 25-45) clients weigh digital savviness and digital tools when choosing a wealth manager/advisor, and how consumers use digital tools in advisor search.

a5.all.label: not_found
a5.all.reason: The passages contain general fee-sensitivity findings (e.g., 62% want fee structure, 73% fee-transparency priority) but none of them break out or mention clients under 40 specifically; no passage addresses how clients under 40 in particular respond to fees, pricing or cost.

first.label: not_found
first.reason: No passage provides evidence about fee/pricing sensitivity specifically for clients under 40. The fee-sensitivity figures (e.g., 48% considering pricing a top factor) are from a survey of all participants and are not broken out by age, and the passages that do mention clients under 40 (Schwab transcripts) concern account opening, not fee sensitivity. The next-generation wealth-manager study lists experience/expertise as the top factor and does not address fees. Thus nothing addresses the age-specific question asked.
