claims.text: UBS research (published April 22, 2026) reports that experience and expertise sit at the top of the next generation's wish list when choosing a wealth manager, cited by 79% of next-generation respondents.
Bank of America Private Bank's 2026 study (published June 17, 2026) reports that 65% of young investors still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor.

A WealthTender survey (published August 13, 2025) found that 73% of people consider fee transparency the most important trust factor when engaging an advisor (all advisor-seekers surveyed, not age-specific).

A WealthTender survey (published August 13, 2025) found the most helpful information when looking for a financial advisor is pricing and fees (70.6%) and years of experience and education (70.8%), followed by specialization (61.0%), professional certifications/credentials (59.6%), and responsiveness/communication style (59.4%); the survey covers all advisor-seekers, not age-specific.

A WealthTender survey (published August 13, 2025) found that people actively considering hiring a financial advisor rely on reviews from actual clients, prefer to speak directly with the advisor (72% visit the advisor's website, 73% schedule an introductory call), and more than half (55%) plan to seek second opinions from others who know the advisors on their shortlist; the survey covers U.S. adults with household incomes over $100,000, ages 35-64, who don't have or are considering changing advisors.

The WealthTender survey (published August 13, 2025) covered 500 U.S. adults with household incomes over $100,000, ages 35-64, screened to include only those who don't currently have an advisor or are considering a change and anticipate hiring within five years.

Among younger investors (Gen Z and Millennials, ages 21 to 45), 65% prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor, while 87% are comfortable with advisors using AI to help manage portfolios (Bank of America Private Bank 2026 study, published June 17, 2026).

The CFPB (published June 6, 2025) reports that younger Americans are far more likely than older Americans to embrace social media, podcasts and generative AI to meet their financial information needs.

The CFPB (published June 6, 2025) reports that Americans aged 25-45 are more trusting than older Americans aged 46-64 of financial information obtained from generative AI tools (44% vs. 26%) and social media (44% vs. 24%).

FINRA (published December 4, 2025) reports that among young investors, word of mouth from friends/family/colleagues is the most frequently mentioned source of investment information, used by 85% of investors under 35.

A Goldman Sachs Asset Management survey (published October 17, 2025) reports that Millennials cite social media more often as a source of information on alternatives, while Boomers rely on traditional outlets.

Schwab CEO Rick Wurster stated (3Q 2025 earnings call, September 30, 2025) that younger investors' top online resource is YouTube, where Schwab is the number one financial services firm by followers, and that younger investors at Schwab are highly engaged in building wealth over the long term.

Wealthtender's 2025 study (published August 13, 2025) of high-income households found that 83% of consumers will research an advisor's reputation online and specifically want to read online reviews (U.S. adults ages 35-64 with $100K+ household income, actively seeking or considering an advisor).

Wealthtender's 2025 study (published August 13, 2025) found that 72% of people will visit the advisor's website to continue their research (U.S. adults ages 35-64 with $100K+ household income, actively seeking or considering an advisor).

In the 2025 Wealthtender Voice of the Client Study (published August 13, 2025), the top financial goals or needs respondents said they would seek a financial advisor's help with were retirement planning and income strategies (63%), investment management and portfolio growth (53%), tax planning and optimization (29%), and estate planning and wealth transfer (26%); the survey covers respondents of all ages.

The Wealthtender study (published August 13, 2025) found that nearly 90% of client reviews about financial advisors focus on relationship quality, planning advice, and emotional factors, while only 1 in 10 centers on investments or portfolio management.

In a Goldman Sachs Asset Management survey (published October 17, 2025), the top three most important investment goals for Millennials (born early 1980s-mid-1990s) were to grow wealth over time, plan for comfortable or early retirement, and achieve financial independence.

Goldman Sachs Asset Management's retirement survey (published October 1, 2025) found that 66% of Gen Z and 59% of Millennials working respondents experienced at least one major life event (such as having a child, buying a home, funding college, or managing a significant financial hardship) in the prior 24 months.

Goldman Sachs Asset Management (published October 1, 2025) reported a generational divide in how competing financial priorities (credit card debt, paying down student loans, saving for college, caring for family members, time out of the workforce, financial hardship) affect retirement savings, with Generation X, Millennials, and Generation Z reporting significantly higher impact than Baby Boomers, and Millennials the most impacted.

Cerulli (published October 29, 2025) found that younger investors typically are more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages, meaning financial advisors looking to connect with these prospective clients must be able to articulate benefits outside of the investing realm, such as financial planning, lending, and tax services.

Fidelity's 2025 Investor Insights Study (published October 9, 2025) found that generation X, Y, and Z investors are reshaping the advisor-client relationship with a focus on holistic financial planning, life goal achievement, and non-traditional investment strategies, and that these wealthy next-generation households seek transparency in advisor compensation and broader life guidance beyond investment management.

A UBS next generation study (published April 22, 2026) found that when choosing a wealth manager, experience and expertise sit at the top of the next generation's wish list (79%), while more than half (56%) want advisors who can build trusted relationships across generations, and 41% value the ability to fully understand the next generation's needs.

A UBS next generation study (published April 22, 2026) found that two-thirds (67%) of next generation investors say a strong personal connection with their advisor is important, and that women place greater weight on personal fit and regular contact while men focus on competitive pricing and specialist expertise.

A Bank of America Private Bank 2026 Study of Wealthy Americans (published June 17, 2026) found that among younger married investors planning is starting earlier: 32% of Gen Z and Millennials have a prenuptial agreement (with another 15% planning to), compared with 15% of Gen X and 4% of Boomers and Silents.

Schwab's CEO Rick Wurster stated (3Q 2025 earnings call, September 30, 2025) that young new-to-firm households (one in three of which are under age 24) come to Schwab wanting to consolidate loans into a Pledged Asset Line to pay off student debt, discuss how to buy a house in the future, and be investors for the long term.
Schwab's CEO Rick Wurster said (2Q 2025 earnings call, June 30, 2025) that young investors come to Schwab wanting to think about how to pay off their college debt and how to buy a house.

Bank of America's investor day (published November 5, 2025) cites McKinsey 2024 survey data that 70% of investors with $250K+ in assets aged 25-44 are looking to transfer investment assets to a bank within the next 12 months.

In the UBS Next Generation study (published April 22, 2026), when the next generation chooses a wealth manager, digital savviness was named by 21% of respondents as a quality a wealth manager should possess, ranking well below experience and expertise (79%) and commitment to next generation (56%); the study notes that technical capability alone isn't enough.

Among younger adults, those aged 25-45 are more trusting than older Americans aged 46-64 of financial information obtained from generative AI tools (44% vs 26%) and social media (44% vs 24%) (CFPB, published June 6, 2025).

Among consumers seeking a financial advisor, 96% said they will do further research online before making a hiring decision, and 83% will research an advisor's reputation by looking for online reviews and awards (Wealthtender study, published August 13, 2025).
A Wealthtender study (published August 13, 2025) found that survey participants said an advisor's physical location doesn't matter because they prefer to meet exclusively online.

The Wealthtender study (published August 13, 2025) describes consumers researching potential advisors using search engines like Google, advisor directories like Wealthtender, and AI tools like ChatGPT.

The Wealthtender study (published August 13, 2025) anticipates continued growth in AI tool usage for advisor searches, increasing expectation for faster response times and digital-first communications, and further acceptance of virtual advisor relationships.
Wealthtender's 2025 study (published August 13, 2025) found that 25% of people plan to use AI-powered tools like ChatGPT or Gemini to start their search for a financial advisor.

A Wealthtender survey (published August 13, 2025) found that 73% of survey participants said transparency in fees and services is crucial for establishing an advisor's credibility (survey respondents, not age-segmented).

Professional certifications/credentials (e.g., CFP, CFA) were cited as most helpful information when looking for a financial advisor by 59.6% of respondents (Wealthtender survey, published August 13, 2025; not age-segmented).
Pushy or aggressive sales tactics were mentioned by 53% of survey participants as a major red flag in choosing an advisor (Wealthtender survey, published August 13, 2025; not age-segmented).

The next generation turns to peers (nearly three in ten) and wealth managers (around two in ten) as their main sources of advice, and prioritizes a close personal relationship alongside strong expertise and experience (UBS next generation research, published April 22, 2026).

The next generation want advisors with not just technical know-how, but the ability to build a rapport with the family and communicate clearly with every generation (UBS next generation research, published April 22, 2026).
UBS's next-generation research (published April 22, 2026) finds the next generation value rapport, with 67% saying a strong personal connection with their advisor is important.

UBS (published April 22, 2026) poses reflective questions to the next generation listing key advisor qualities: technical expertise, personal rapport, long-term support, or access to wider networks and opportunities.

Wealthtender's survey (published August 13, 2025) found that 63% of people consider professional credentials like CFP or CFA a key factor in determining an advisor's trustworthiness (ages 35-64, $100K+ household income).
Bank of America Private Bank's 2026 Study of Wealthy Americans (published June 17, 2026) found that 47% of young investors use AI to research companies or markets.
Schwab stated (2Q 2026 earnings call, June 30, 2026) that 61% of affluent clients ages 25 to 44 prefer to consolidate their wealth and banking relationships.

Cerulli Associates research (published October 29, 2025) notes that, while older investors tend to be more advisor-reliant, younger investors prefer to retain a greater degree of control of at least part of their investing lives.

Wealthtender's advisor-search survey (published August 13, 2025) reports that clients seeking to hire a financial advisor should start with referrals from trusted friends, family members and professionals, then use online resources to research and read reviews, and evaluate multiple advisors before deciding (Americans seeking to hire an advisor, all ages, not specifically under 40).

The Wealthtender study (published August 13, 2025) surveyed 500 U.S. adults with household incomes over $100,000, ages 35-64, who are actively considering or planning to hire an advisor; it focuses on this 35-64 age group rather than clients under 40.
The Wealthtender study (published August 13, 2025) describes its focus as the 35-64 age group with $100K+ incomes, not clients under 40.
Bank of America's investor day (published November 5, 2025) cites that 70% of next-gen clients seek to consolidate banking/lending and investments relationships to a bank in the next year.
Bank of America Private Bank's 2026 Study of Wealthy Americans (published June 17, 2026) found that 47% of young investors use AI to research companies or markets (2026).
UBS research (published April 22, 2026) found that younger adults (22 to 25 years) rely most on peers (57%) for advice in the context of succession planning (2026).

Bank of America Private Bank's 2024 Study of Wealthy Americans (published June 18, 2024) found a generational divide, with Millennials and Gen Z allocating three times more of their investment portfolios to alternative investments than older generations (2024; Millennials and Gen Z basis).

Bank of America Private Bank's 2026 Study of Wealthy Americans (published June 17, 2026) reports that 65% of younger investors (Gen Z and Millennials, ages 21 to 45) still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor. Why it might matter: in the same passage, the study reports that 47% of young investors use AI to research companies or markets and 87% are comfortable with advisors using AI to help manage portfolios, so the 65% preference for a human advisor persists despite broad AI comfort.

Bank of America Private Bank's 2026 Study of Wealthy Americans (published June 17, 2026) found that 65% of young investors (Gen Z / Millennials) still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor, even as most are comfortable with advisors using AI. Why it might matter: the same passage reports that 47% of young investors use AI to research companies or markets and 87% are comfortable with advisors using AI to help manage portfolios, yet 65% still prefer a human advisor.

Among the next generation, younger adults (ages 22 to 25) rely most on their peers (57%) as their most important source of advice when making succession-planning decisions (UBS, published April 22, 2026). Why it might matter: the same UBS passage reports that older respondents turn increasingly to formal legal advice, with those above 45 most likely to consult lawyers (67%), showing the peer reliance is specific to younger adults.

Bank of America's 2025 investor-day deck (published November 5, 2025), citing McKinsey (2024), states that 70% of investors aged 25-44 with $250K+ in investable assets are looking to transfer investment assets to a bank within the next 12 months. Why it might matter: the same investor-day slide also cites McKinsey data that 60% of $5-25MM investors aged 45-64 prefer to consolidate investments and banking relationships, underscoring a broader consolidation priority across age groups.

Schwab states (3Q 2025 earnings call, September 30, 2025) that Gen Z investors (ages 13 to 28) learn about finances primarily through social media and family, and that Schwab meets them in those channels. Why it might matter: in the same statement, Schwab's CEO says meeting Gen Z in those channels is one of the reasons they are turning to Schwab.

Wealthy next-generation (Gen X, Y, and Z) high-net-worth households seek transparency in advisor compensation, broader life guidance beyond investment management, and emerging investment products, and are reshaping the advisor-client relationship around holistic financial planning and life-goal achievement (Fidelity 2025 Investor Insights Study, published October 9, 2025). Why it might matter: Fidelity's passage frames this against the largest wealth transfer in history, as generation X, Y, and Z investors reshape the advisor-client relationship.

The CFPB (published June 6, 2025) reports that Millennials and Gen Z are more likely than older adults to act on financial information they encounter without further validation, especially from online sources. Why it might matter: the same CFPB passage reports that those aged 25-45 are more trusting than older Americans aged 46-64 of financial information from generative AI tools (44% vs. 26%) and social media (44% vs. 24%), so younger clients are especially exposed to unvalidated online information.

a3.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley's integrated-firm client journey includes 'Founders Wealth Strategies' capabilities and, under 'Preserve Wealth,' 'Full-Service Wealth Advice and Asset Allocation' and 'Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning,' indicating the firm retains wealth across generations through family office, trust and estate planning services.
items.quote: Founders Wealth Strategies ... Preserve Wealth ... Full-Service Wealth Advice and Asset Allocation ... Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning

items.text: Morgan Stanley is investing to broaden capabilities for its financial advisors that include 'family office and OCIO,' alongside alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets and tailored lending, which support retaining multi-generational wealth.
items.quote: We are using our scale to invest in broadening capabilities for FAs that are difficult for others to replicate: alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending.

a3.MS.reason: The passages describe the firm's family office, trust & estate planning, and founders wealth strategies as capabilities used to preserve and retain wealth, which directly addresses preparing for wealth passing to heirs.

a4.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley's Wealth Management had 15,950 Wealth Management representatives (financial advisors) as of December 31, 2020.
items.quote: Wealth Management representatives 15,950 15,469 15,468 3% 3%

items.text: Morgan Stanley's Wealth Management had 15,469 Wealth Management representatives as of September 30, 2020.
items.quote: Wealth Management representatives 15,950 15,469 15,468 3% 3%

items.text: Morgan Stanley's Wealth Management had 15,468 Wealth Management representatives as of December 31, 2019.
items.quote: Wealth Management representatives 15,950 15,469 15,468 3% 3%

items.text: Morgan Stanley for years has deferred a small amount of each advisor's gross revenue as 'deferred compensation' and required advisors to stay at the firm for years in order to vest, a retention mechanism known as 'golden handcuffs'.
items.quote: Giants like Morgan Stanley for years have taken a small amount of an advisor's gross revenue, called it deferred compensation, and required advisors to stay for years in order to vest.

items.text: Morgan Stanley is not introducing retention bonuses as part of its 2027 pay plan for advisors, but is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, so advisors must generate that much more revenue to receive the same pay.
items.quote: Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, meaning advisors have to generate that much more revenue to see the same pay next year.

items.text: Morgan Stanley will increase the cash component of its advisor compensation as it transitions deferred compensation plan (DCP) economic hedges to derivative instruments, changes it says support its overall investment into its financial advisors and simplify its compensation program.
items.quote: we will also increase the cash component of our advisor compensation... these changes support our overall investment into our financial advisors and will help simplify our compensation program.

items.text: Morgan Stanley states its ability to retain and attract qualified employees is critical to its success, and that failure to attract, integrate, and retain highly qualified employees or successfully transition key roles may materially adversely affect its performance.
items.quote: If we are unable to continue to attract, integrate and retain highly qualified employees or successfully transition key roles, or do so at levels or in forms necessary to maintain our competitive position, our performance, including our competitive position and results of operations, could be materially adversely affected.

items.text: Morgan Stanley notes advisor-led flows were particularly strong, originating from new advisors attracted to the strength of the workplace channel.
items.quote: Advisor-led flows were particularly strong, originating from new advisors who are attracted to the strength of the workplace, as well as assets that originated from workplace.

a4.MS.reason: Passages state Morgan Stanley's advisor headcount figures (2020 supplement) and its advisor retention/compensation/succession-related measures, which directly address how it manages its advisor force.

a5.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley's strategic update deck shows the firm serves founders and employees across their growth cycle (from early stage through public company) with offerings including Founders Wealth Strategies, Private Shares Trading & Lending, IPO Execution and Support Services, Financial Wellness and Employee Benefits, Full-Service Wealth Advice and Asset Allocation, Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning, and Unlock Liquidity.
items.quote: Corporates / Founders / Employees / Early Stage / Public Company / Invest for the Future / Financial Wellness and Employee Benefits / Founders Wealth Strategies / Preserve Wealth / Full-Service Wealth Advice and Asset Allocation / Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning / Unlock Liquidity / Private Shares Trading & Lending / IPO Execution and Support Services / Optimize for Growth

items.text: Morgan Stanley states it is using scale to invest in broadening capabilities for financial advisors, including alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending.
items.quote: We are using our scale to invest in broadening capabilities for FAs that are difficult for others to replicate: alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending.

items.text: Morgan Stanley reports it continues to invest to deepen competitive moats, including an expanded collaboration with Carta in private markets and in digital assets through announced partnerships with Zero Hash.
items.quote: we continue to invest, deepening our competitive moats in areas like our expanded collaboration with Carta in private markets and in digital assets through announced partnerships with Zero Hash.

items.text: Morgan Stanley identifies strategic initiatives such as its acquisition of EquityZen, expanded partnership with Carta, and collaboration with Zero Hash as reflecting its commitment to innovation and to introduce and educate retail clients to the value of advice.
items.quote: Strategic initiatives such as our recent acquisition of EquityZen, expanded partnership with Carta, and collaboration with Zero Hash all reflect our commitment to innovation... Our intentional strategy to introduce and educate retail clients to the value of advice

items.text: Morgan Stanley describes the early days of its digital asset transformation in wealth, including a partnership with Zero Hash, expansion into crypto and tokenized asset space, and continued work in E*TRADE for its active self-directed community.
items.quote: I would also call out just the early days of the digital asset transformation side of wealth. We announced a partnership with Zero Hash last year... We're well positioned now in the crypto and tokenized asset space... There is continued work that we're doing in E*TRADE

items.text: Morgan Stanley states its ability to serve clients across the private to public continuum continues to attract assets to its platform, delivering unique products, solutions, and advice, with growth led by workplace relationships from large IPOs of late-stage private workplace clients.
items.quote: Our ability to serve clients across the private to public continuum continues to attract assets to our world- class platform, delivering unique products, solutions, and advice.

a5.MS.reason: The passages describe specific products, services and platforms Morgan Stanley offers to attract and serve next-generation (founder/employee/early-stage) clients, so these are facts.

a6.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley's integrated firm capabilities chart lists 'Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning' among the offerings under the 'Preserve Wealth' stage of serving clients throughout their growth cycles.
items.quote: Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning

items.text: Morgan Stanley's CEO states that as a Morgan Stanley client you have access to ultra-high net worth family office infrastructure solutions.
items.quote: importantly, for ultra-high net worth family office infrastructure solutions

items.text: Morgan Stanley's CFO states the firm has done a lot of work on trying to service founders and family offices as part of growing its Wealth Management business.
items.quote: We've done a lot of work on trying to service founders, on trying to service family offices.

items.text: Morgan Stanley's CEO lists 'family office and OCIO' among the capabilities the firm is investing in for financial advisors that are difficult for others to replicate.
items.quote: alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending

a6.MS.reason: The deck and transcripts describe family office solutions, trust and estate planning, and servicing family offices, which directly bear on engaging families and multi-generational wealth planning.

a7.MS.label: fact

items.text: Chairman and CEO Ted Pick said Morgan Stanley is focused on both public and private ecosystems, and that the objective is to cover growth companies and their employees from founding to their public maturity while broadening investor access to private companies.
items.quote: We are focused on both the public and the private ecosystems, augmented by our recent acquisition of EquityZen. The objective is to cover growth companies and their employees from founding to their public maturity while broadening access for investors to the growing stack of private companies.

items.text: Morgan Stanley's strategic update deck lays out an integrated-firm capability map spanning Corporates, Founders/Employees, Early Stage, and Public Company, including 'Founders Wealth Strategies,' 'Preserve Wealth,' and 'Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning.'
items.quote: Corporates / Founders / Employees / Early Stage / Public Company ... Financial Wellness and Employee Benefits ... Founders Wealth Strategies ... Preserve Wealth ... Full-Service Wealth Advice and Asset Allocation ... Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning

items.text: Ted Pick said the Morgan Stanley at Work business, with its exclusive partnership with Carta, positions the firm as an early trusted advisor to over 50,000 private companies, and that employees across workplace companies benefit from management of equity compensation plans, liquidity opportunities, and full-service advice.
items.quote: Our Morgan Stanley at Work business, with its exclusive partnership with Carta, positions us as an early trusted advisor to over 50,000 private companies.

items.text: CFO Sharon Yeshaya said Morgan Stanley has an exclusive partnership with Carta under which Carta will refer private stock-plan companies to Morgan Stanley as they move toward going public, creating a seamless experience for those clients.
items.quote: we have an exclusive partnership with Carta, which means that they will refer those private different stock plans or different corporate companies to Morgan Stanley as they move into going public.

items.text: CFO Sharon Yeshaya described how Morgan Stanley understands the full cap table and early investors, so that IPO-related flows (e.g., an endowment receiving stock) can move from a transfer agent into a Morgan Stanley advice-based relationship across different portions of the cap table.
items.quote: we have a full cap table. We understand early investors. And you can think, for example, of an endowment that might receive a stock associated with an IPO. He or she might take that and put it through from a transfer agent into a Morgan Stanley advice-based relationship.

items.text: Ted Pick said Morgan Stanley is using its scale to invest in broadening financial advisor capabilities including family office and OCIO, tailored lending, alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, and digitized assets.
items.quote: We are using our scale to invest in broadening capabilities for FAs that are difficult for others to replicate: alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending.

a7.MS.reason: Passages contain leadership statements and strategic initiatives (integrated firm covering founders/employees through public maturity, Carta partnership, EquityZen, family office/trust and estate planning, IPO cap-table capture) that indicate commitment to capturing wealth transfer.

This comparison cannot be validly made on a single common basis from the disclosed figures, because the five firms disclose different and non-comparable metrics and definitions for wealth-transfer preparedness. Schwab is the only firm that quantifies a direct wealth-transfer retention rate (~75% of assets retained in a wealth transfer event) alongside a next-gen acquisition figure (~70% of new-to-firm retail households are Gen Z/Millennials); Morgan Stanley discloses 99% client retention and 60% of advisor-led assets tied to 20-year relationships plus family-office/OCIO capabilities; Edward Jones frames the wealth transfer as a risk and discloses advisor attrition and a next-gen digital platform; Merrill discloses next-gen advisor rankings and GWIM net client AUM flows (with GWIM including Bank of America Private Bank, not Merrill alone); and Raymond James discloses domestic PCG net new assets and a private-wealth advisor designation program. Because there is no shared metric across the five, no firm can be ranked as 'most prepared' on the disclosed figures; Schwab's direct wealth-transfer retention rate is the most direct disclosed evidence but is not comparable to the other firms' proxy figures.

(SCHW-10K-2025#119) | Edward Jones: 'Net new assets represents cash and securities inflows and outflows, including fees and commissions and excluding mutual fund capital gain distributions...' (EDJ-10Q-2026Q2#60) | Merrill (Bank of America Corporation): defines a related metric instead: 'The net client AUM flows represent the net change in clients’ AUM balances over a specified period of time, excluding market appreciation/depreciation and...' (BAC-10K-2025#249) | Raymond James Financial: 'Domestic PCG net new assets represents domestic PCG client inflows, including dividends and interest, less domestic PCG client outflows, including commissions,...' (RJF-10K-2025#224).

The client assets per advisor figures cannot be validly compared side by side across the five firms. The client asset measures differ in definition: Morgan Stanley's client assets is the sum of Wealth Management client assets and Investment Management AUM, with its advisor-led channel (client assets in accounts with a Wealth Management representative assigned) of $5,715 billion at December 31, 2025 excluding self-directed and workplace channels; Schwab's total client assets span brokerage accounts, workplace plan participant accounts, banking accounts, and custodial assets held for independent advisors; Edward Jones uses client assets under care (AUC); Merrill uses client balances composed of assets under management, brokerage and other assets, deposits, and loans and leases; and Raymond James uses client assets under administration (AUA), itself cautioning that 'The definitions for client assets may be inconsistent across companies.' The advisor counts also differ in definition: Morgan Stanley reports Wealth Management representatives (15,950 at December 31, 2020); Schwab reports no financial-advisor headcount (only approximately 4,127 employees performing investment advisory functions, more than 16,000 independent RIA firms, or approximately 33,000 full-time employees); Edward Jones reports financial advisors (actual), distinct from a full-time equivalent basis; Merrill's available count spans all wealth management businesses in GWIM and Consumer Banking (or Merrill plus Private Bank), not Merrill alone; and Raymond James counts employee and independent contractor advisors while excluding RCS-division advisors whose assets are nonetheless included in AUA. Because the numerators, denominators, and their definitions all differ, and because the per-advisor figures are stand-in components rather than a shared disclosed metric, the figures are not on the same basis and cannot be validly compared.

a1.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley discloses that for certain revenue-producing employees in its Wealth Management and Investment Management segments, compensation is largely paid on the basis of formulaic payouts that link employee compensation to revenues.
items.quote: For certain revenue-producing employees in the Wealth Management and Investment Management business segments, compensation is largely paid on the basis of formulaic payouts that link employee compensation to revenues.
items.scope: Wealth Management and Investment Management segments

items.text: Morgan Stanley attributes increased compensation and benefits expenses in part to an increase in the formulaic payout to Wealth Management advisors on higher revenues/compensable revenue.
items.quote: Compensation and benefits expenses of $29,216 million in 2025 increased 12% from the prior year, primarily due to an increase in the formulaic payout to Wealth Management advisors and higher discretionary incentive compensation within Institutional Securities, both on higher revenues, and higher salary expenses.

items.text: Morgan Stanley states it will increase the cash component of its advisor compensation and that it is transitioning all economic hedges for deferred cash-based compensation (DCP) obligations to derivative instruments.
items.quote: we will also increase the cash component of our advisor compensation. We are making these changes to reduce the accounting-driven volatility in revenues and earnings.

items.text: Morgan Stanley discloses that the amount of the client fee is a factor used in calculating the compensation paid to the Financial Advisor, and that if the fee rate is below a certain threshold the advisor is given credit for less than the total fee, giving advisors a financial incentive not to reduce fees below that threshold.
items.quote: The amount of the fee you pay is a factor we use in calculating the compensation we pay your Financial Advisor. ... If your fee rate is below a certain threshold, we give your Financial Advisor credit for less than the total amount of your fee in calculating his or her compensation.

items.text: Morgan Stanley discloses that a Morgan Stanley Virtual Advisor (MSVA) is paid a base salary plus a discretionary bonus and does not retain any portion of the Morgan Stanley Advisory Fee.
items.quote: If your account is serviced through a Morgan Stanley Virtual Advisor ("MSVA"), your MSVA is paid a base salary plus a discretionary bonus and does not retain any portion of the Morgan Stanley Advisory Fee.

items.text: Morgan Stanley discloses that a portion of the Morgan Stanley Advisory Fee is paid to the client's Financial Advisor.
items.quote: A portion of the Morgan Stanley Advisory Fee will be paid to your Financial Advisor.

items.text: Morgan Stanley discloses that Financial Advisors and their Branch Managers receive no additional compensation as a result of certain payments (brokerage commissions, revenue-sharing, administrative service fees, expense reimbursement and data analytics fees) received by Morgan Stanley from certain Funds.
items.quote: Financial Advisors and their Branch Managers receive no additional compensation as a result of these payments received by Morgan Stanley.

items.text: Morgan Stanley discloses that Financial Advisors in advisory programs do not receive additional compensation as a result of revenue sharing support fees, mutual fund administrative service fees and data analytics payments received by Morgan Stanley.
items.quote: To mitigate these conflicts, Financial Advisors in advisory programs do not receive additional compensation as a result of the support fees, mutual fund administrative service fees and data analytics payments received by Morgan Stanley.

items.text: Morgan Stanley has taken a small amount of an advisor's gross revenue as deferred compensation, requiring advisors to stay at the firm for years to vest (golden handcuffs).
items.quote: Giants like Morgan Stanley for years have taken a small amount of an advisor's gross revenue, called it deferred compensation, and required advisors to stay for years in order to vest.

items.text: Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, meaning advisors have to generate that much more revenue to see the same pay next year; the firm is not introducing retention bonuses as part of its 2027 pay plan.
items.quote: Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, meaning advisors have to generate that much more revenue to see the same pay next year.

items.text: Morgan Stanley describes its compensation programs (which vary by location) as including, in addition to salaries, annual bonuses, retirement savings plans with matching contributions, an employee stock purchase plan, student loan refinancing and a financial wellbeing program.
items.quote: In addition to salaries, these programs (which vary by location) include annual bonuses, retirement savings plans with matching contributions, an employee stock purchase plan, student loan refinancing and a financial wellbeing program.

a1.MS.reason: The passages contain multiple direct disclosures of Morgan Stanley's advisor compensation structure, including formulaic payouts, deferred compensation, cash component, fee-based compensation factors, and the MSVA salary-plus-bonus structure.

They also earn compensation based on the revenue that Merrill earns from Sales Charges related to securities transactions in any brokerage account you may have as well as from the revenue derived from the referrals to Affiliates (including referrals to an Affiliate for banking products or services).

items.text: Merrill discloses that Advisors receive production credits toward their compensation formula based on the Merrill Lynch Fee, and that Advisors receive 10% or more fewer production credits if the weighted average Merrill Lynch Fee Rate for a client's Accounts (and Household Accounts) falls below rate levels for specific wealth asset tiers Merrill establishes.
items.quote: In general, Advisors receive "production credits" toward their compensation formula based on the amount of the Merrill Lynch Fee that you pay for your Account. Merrill's policies result in Advisors receiving fewer production credits (by 10% or more) if the weighted average of the Merrill Lynch Fee Rates for a client's Accounts and for Accounts that are part of the Household is lower than the rate levels for specific wealth asset tiers that Merrill establishes.

items.text: Merrill discloses that the higher the Merrill Lynch Fee Rate a client agrees to, the more the Advisor earns in production credits, and the more production credits an Advisor generates, the higher the Advisor's incentive compensation.
items.quote: The higher the Merrill Lynch Fee Rate you agree to, the more your Advisor earns in production credits. The more overall production credits that an Advisor generates, the higher the Advisor's incentive compensation.

items.text: Merrill discloses that Advisors are eligible for a compensation award, payable over a defined period, from an incentive program based on meeting prior-year growth targets in new households and in assets and liabilities (including investment activity, new trust accounts, 401(k) accounts, and banking/lending participation), and that an Advisor's incentive compensation grid is reduced if they fail to achieve growth for two consecutive years in the assets and liabilities component.
items.quote: Advisors are eligible to receive a compensation award, payable over a defined period of time, from an incentive program that is currently based on meeting growth targets from the prior year in new households and in assets and liabilities. ... An Advisor is subject to a reduction in their incentive compensation grid if they fail to achieve growth for two consecutive years in the assets and liabilities component of the award.

items.text: Merrill discloses that Advisors who join from other firms generally receive recruitment payments that may take forms including salary guarantees, upfront awards, and compensation contingent on continued employment such as deferred payments and recruitment loans, generally based largely on the size of their prior business, and that these bonuses are in addition to their incentive compensation.
items.quote: Advisors who join Merrill from other firms generally receive payments in connection with that move. These payments may take various forms, including salary guarantees, upfront awards and various forms of compensation contingent on continued employment (e.g., deferred payments, recruitment loans). ... These bonuses are in addition to the incentive compensation to which they are otherwise entitled as Advisors.

items.text: Merrill discloses that elements of its field management compensation are based on revenues to Merrill and on the financial advisors they manage meeting strategic goals set for the year, and that Merrill management and other employees receive incentive compensation based on factors including the profitability of Merrill and BofA Corp.
items.quote: Elements of our field management compensation are based on revenues to Merrill and based on the financial advisors whom they manage meeting strategic goals set for the year, including the growth in assets and liabilities component of the award as described in the subsection "Advisor Compensation and Awards." Management personnel of Merrill and other employees of Merrill, MAA and their Affiliates receive incentive compensation based on a number of factors including the profitability of Merrill and BofA Corp.

items.text: Merrill's Advisor Development Program web page discloses that advisor roles include a base salary and unlimited earning potential.
items.quote: Base salary and unlimited earning potential

items.text: Merrill discloses that for Program Accounts, Advisors are compensated based on the Merrill Lynch Fee charged on the Account (based on the agreed-upon fee rate and asset value including cash), and that Advisors receive increased compensation for achieving strategic objectives such as growth in clients' participation in banking services and Lending Programs, but do not receive additional compensation for advisory client assets held in the Cash Sweep Program.
items.quote: For Program Accounts, Advisors are compensated based on the Merrill Lynch Fee charged on the Account which is based on the agreed-upon Merrill Lynch Fee Rate and the value of the assets in the Account, including cash balances and cash alternatives swept under the Cash Sweep Program. ... Advisors do not receive additional compensation as a result of advisory client assets held in the Cash Sweep Program.

items.text: Merrill discloses that it calculates the compensation paid to its Advisors on the same basis for all Program assets and without regard to the amount of any additional compensation Merrill or its Affiliates receive in connection with certain investments, and that Advisors do not receive any portion of, or credit for, compensation paid to Merrill or its Affiliates.

A comparison of the level of detail each firm discloses about advisor compensation can be made on this evidence, but only qualitatively, not on a like-for-like numeric basis. Raymond James is the only one of the five that discloses specific numeric payout rates or ranges (up to 50% for Traditional Employee, 70–80% gross for Advisor Select, and 81%–90% for Independent Contractor and Corporate RIA, per its affiliation-options webpage). Because the firms disclose different elements (numeric grids versus qualitative structures versus company-wide packages), a numeric comparison of payout levels across all five is not valid.

duplicates_removed.text: Edward Jones: In its 2026 Form ADV (published March 27, 2026), Edward Jones states that most financial advisors are eligible to participate in the Edward Jones Travel Award Program, with eligibility based upon the amount of new and existing assets under care of a financial advisor.

Merrill: In its 2026 Form ADV (published October 30, 2026), Merrill discloses it pays Advisors a salary and incentive compensation based on the revenues Merrill receives for providing Program Services and brokerage services; Advisors are credited with 'production credits' from a portion of the Merrill Lynch Fee and Sales Charges, plus credits for margin lending, cash swept to Bank Affiliates, and referrals for banking, lending and other financial services.

Morgan Stanley: In its 2025 Form 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025), Morgan Stanley states that for certain revenue-producing employees in its Wealth Management and Investment Management business segments, compensation is largely paid on the basis of formulaic payouts that link employee compensation to revenues: "For certain revenue-producing employees in the Wealth Management and Investment Management business segments, compensation is largely paid on the basis of formulaic payouts that link employee compensation to revenues."

Morgan Stanley: In its 2026 Form ADV (published November 4, 2026), Morgan Stanley states that a Financial Advisor serviced through a Morgan Stanley Virtual Advisor is paid a base salary plus a discretionary bonus and does not retain any portion of the Morgan Stanley Advisory Fee.

Morgan Stanley: In its 2026 Form ADV (published November 4, 2026), Morgan Stanley states that the amount of the client fee is a factor used in calculating Financial Advisor compensation, and that if the fee rate is below a certain threshold the advisor is given credit for less than the total amount of the fee.

Morgan Stanley: In its 2026 Form ADV (published November 4, 2026), Morgan Stanley states that Financial Advisors in advisory programs do not receive additional compensation as a result of the support fees, mutual fund administrative service fees and data analytics payments received by Morgan Stanley.

Morgan Stanley: Trade press (October 26, 2026) reports that Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, meaning advisors must generate that much more revenue to receive the same pay next year.
Raymond James Financial: For the Advisor Select affiliation model, Raymond James discloses a 70-80% gross payout (webpage, page content as of April 21, 2026).

Morgan Stanley: In its 2026 Form ADV (published November 4, 2026), Morgan Stanley discloses that a Morgan Stanley Virtual Advisor is paid a base salary plus a discretionary bonus and does not retain any portion of the Morgan Stanley Advisory Fee: "your MSVA is paid a base salary plus a discretionary bonus and does not retain any portion of the Morgan Stanley Advisory Fee."

The Charles Schwab Corporation: In its 2025 Form 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025), Schwab discloses that its employee compensation package includes performance-based incentive pay, equity awards, and recognition awards in addition to base pay.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: In its 2025 Form 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025), Schwab discloses that its 2022 Stock Incentive Plan provides for granting stock options and restricted stock units to employees and non-employee directors.

Edward Jones: In its 2026 Form ADV (published March 27, 2026), Edward Jones states that the Program Fee, assets under care, and Reserve Line Advance balances will impact most financial advisors' eligibility for a bonus and bonus amount.

Merrill: In its 2026 Form ADV (published October 30, 2026), Merrill states that an Advisor is subject to a reduction in their incentive compensation grid if they fail to achieve growth for two consecutive years in the assets and liabilities component of the award, and that Merrill considers and approves its compensation program from year to year.

Merrill: In its 2026 Form ADV (published October 30, 2026), Merrill discloses that advisors who join from other firms generally receive payments in connection with the move, which may take various forms including salary guarantees, upfront awards, and various forms of compensation contingent on continued employment such as deferred payments and recruitment loans. Why it might matter: the passage notes the future payments based on assets that transfer create a conflict of interest since the Advisor has an incentive to recommend that the client transfer assets to Merrill.

Morgan Stanley: Trade press (October 26, 2026) reports Morgan Stanley is not introducing retention bonuses as part of its 2027 pay plan for advisors and is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027. Why it might matter: the trade press article reports that Morgan Stanley and Merrill Lynch are not introducing retention bonuses as part of their 2027 pay plans, adhering to a more traditional approach.

Morgan Stanley: Trade press (October 26, 2026) reports Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, meaning advisors have to generate that much more revenue to see the same pay next year. Why it might matter: the article notes Merrill Lynch is leaving its core pay plan for advisors, known in the industry as the grid, unchanged for next year, while Morgan Stanley raises its pay threshold.

Morgan Stanley: On its 4Q25 earnings call (January 15, 2026), Morgan Stanley stated it will increase the cash component of its advisor compensation. Why it might matter: Morgan Stanley stated it is making these changes to reduce the accounting-driven volatility in revenues and earnings and to help simplify its compensation program.

Financial advisor attrition was 6.1% as a result of a variety of factors, including a rise in financial advisor departures with tenure of five years or less."

Edward Jones: The 10-Q for the period ended June 27, 2025 (published August 8, 2025) states "The Partnership ended the second quarter with 20,309 financial advisors. Financial advisor attrition increased to 6.4% primarily due to an increase in retirements, consistent with industry trends."

Edward Jones: The 10-Q for the period ended September 26, 2025 reports financial advisor attrition of 6.0% for the nine months ended September 26, 2025, compared with 5.1% for the nine months ended September 27, 2024, and 4.7% for the third quarter of 2024.

Edward Jones: The 10-Qs for the periods ended September 26, 2025 and June 27, 2025 define "Attrition %" as "the annualized number of financial advisors that left or retired from the Partnership during the period compared to the total number of financial advisors as of period end."

Edward Jones and Merrill: On this evidence, Edward Jones's advisor attrition rate cannot be compared to Merrill's. Edward Jones discloses a numeric attrition rate — 6.1% in the third quarter of 2025 and 6.4% in the second quarter of 2025 — defined in its 10-Qs as "the annualized number of financial advisors that left or retired from the Partnership during the period compared to the total number of financial advisors as of period end." Merrill discloses no numeric attrition rate: Bank of America's CFO stated only that "adviser attrition is now at near historic lows" (transcript for the period ended June 30, 2026, published July 14, 2026). Edward Jones's 10-K for the period ended December 31, 2025 additionally states "the Partnership believes its rate of attrition of financial advisors is in line with comparable firms." Because Merrill reports no numeric advisor attrition rate, the two firms' attrition rates cannot be compared on this evidence.
